prompt: You run `az account show` in a terminal set up as this course says, and it answers `Please run 'az login' to setup account.` What does that tell you?
hint: Ask what the CLI did before it would have sent anything.

choices.text: The lab works, and the CLI stopped before sending anything
choices.why: Right. That refusal is the answer every subscription command gets in this course.

choices.text: The installation is broken and has to be run again from the start
choices.why: A broken install fails earlier, with `az: command not found` or a Python error, not with a request to sign in.

choices.text: Azure rejected the request because the course's subscription has expired
choices.why: There is no subscription in this course, and nothing reached Azure: the CLI refused on its own.

choices.text: You are now expected to run `az login` to be able to continue the lesson
choices.why: That would open a real Microsoft sign-in, and the course assumes the CLI has nobody to act for.

prompt: A new terminal answers `bash: line 1: az: command not found`, although the install finished yesterday. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What do the four terminal lines do?

choices.text: The virtual environment in `~/azure/venv` was deleted overnight by a clean-up job
choices.why: Nothing deletes it; a new terminal simply does not know where it is until you tell it.

choices.text: The four lines that start every working terminal were not typed in this one
choices.why: Right. They activate the virtual environment and put `az` and `bicep` on the path, and every new terminal starts without them.

choices.text: Docker is not running
choices.why: Docker has nothing to do with finding `az`; a stopped daemon gives a different message about its socket.

choices.text: The CLI needs `az login` before it will start
choices.why: The CLI starts without an account and refuses only the commands that need one.

prompt: `echo $AZURE_DEFAULTS_LOCATION` prints an empty line. What goes wrong later if you carry on?
hint: Which commands read that variable?

choices.text: Bicep refuses each file, because it needs a region to compile
choices.why: The compiler does not read the variable; a file's location comes from the file.

choices.text: No harm, since the course's commands take no region
choices.why: Plenty do: every command that takes a location and was not given one reads this variable.

choices.text: Commands given no location have no region to fall back on
choices.why: Right. The fourth terminal line sets `brazilsouth` as the default, and an empty line means it was missed.

choices.text: Docker starts pulling its images from a mirror outside Brazil
choices.why: Docker does not read Azure's variables; where images come from is the daemon's configuration.

prompt: The CLI and the Bicep compiler are installed in a Python ___ environment of their own, so they touch nothing else on the machine.
hint: The directory is called `venv`.

prompt: Which of these does the lab give you? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three tools and Docker, and no account.

choices.text: The real Azure CLI, answering from its own help and offline lists
choices.why: Yes. Version 2.91.0, the same CLI you would use against a subscription.

choices.text: A local imitation of Resource Manager that creates virtual machines
choices.why: No such thing exists for Azure, which is the point of the section.

choices.text: A Bicep compiler that checks declarations against Azure's resource types
choices.why: Yes, offline, and it is the closest thing to Azure the course has.

choices.text: Docker, to run the images Azure would run and Microsoft's emulators
choices.why: Yes, the one the `docker` course installed.

choices.text: A free trial subscription that expires when the course ends
choices.why: There is no subscription of any kind; nothing in the course is billed.

prompt: A section on scale set upgrades shows `az vmss update ...` with no output under it. What does that tell you?
hint: There are two kinds of section.

choices.text: The command ran and printed an empty result
choices.why: It never ran: it needs a subscription, and a read section says so rather than invent an answer.

choices.text: The lab ran it against an emulator with no output
choices.why: No emulator answers Azure's control plane, and scale sets are control plane.

choices.text: The output was removed to keep the section short
choices.why: Captured output is never trimmed away; a practised section pastes it as the machine printed it.

choices.text: A read section: it was never run
choices.why: Right. Any output shown there would have been invented.

prompt: `bicep build` prints a BCP089 warning about a misspelt property, and `check.json` appears anyway. What does the course ask you to do?
hint: What is the strongest check you can make without a subscription?

choices.text: Treat it as a refusal and fix the file until it compiles with no warnings
choices.why: Right. A declaration is finished in this course when it compiles clean.

choices.text: Delete `check.json`, because a warning means the file is not valid JSON in the first place
choices.why: The JSON is well formed; the warning is about what it says, not about its syntax.

choices.text: Deploy the template, since the compiler merely warned
choices.why: Azure might drop the misspelt property in silence, and you would get a resource without what you asked for.

choices.text: Report it as a type inaccuracy, as the message suggests
choices.why: That link is for when Microsoft's types are wrong. Here the file was wrong, and the compiler even names the right spelling.

prompt: A Bicep file for a VM compiles with no warnings. Which question is still open?
hint: What does the compiler compare a file against?

choices.text: Whether the property names are spelt as Azure expects
choices.why: That is exactly what it checks, against the published types, and it would have warned.

choices.text: Whether a number was written where text belongs
choices.why: A type mismatch is a BCP036 warning, and there were none.

choices.text: Whether the file is valid Bicep syntax
choices.why: A syntax error stops compilation outright; it compiled.

choices.text: Whether the region offers it within quota
choices.why: Right. Only Azure answers that, at deployment.

prompt: Which of these could this course show you as a real transcript? Choose all that apply.
hint: Practised means recorded in the lab; read means taught from the documentation.

choices.text: The help text of `az vm create`
choices.why: Yes. The CLI prints its help without an account.

choices.text: A container running the shop's image
choices.why: Yes. Docker runs the same image Azure would, from lesson 7.

choices.text: The JSON Azure returns after creating a virtual machine
choices.why: That needs Resource Manager, and nothing on a laptop answers it.

choices.text: A Spot machine being evicted
choices.why: Eviction is the control plane at work; lesson 5 teaches it by reading.

choices.text: The compiler's warnings on a misspelt property
choices.why: Yes. That runs offline, and the section shows it.

prompt: Put the life of a Bicep declaration in this course in order, from writing it to the first answer only Azure can give.
hint: The compiler comes before anything Azure decides.
items: Write the resource with its type and API version
Fix the file until the compiler has no warnings
Deploy it, which is where offer and quota are decided
trap: Deploying straight after a build with warnings skips the one check you can make on a laptop.

prompt: Match each piece of `Standard_E8as_v5` to what it says.
hint: Family, vCPUs, processor, storage, version.

prompt: What processor does `Standard_D2s_v5` run on?
hint: Look for a processor letter after the number.

choices.text: AMD, the default for the D family
choices.why: AMD is spelt with an `a`, as in `D2as_v5`.

choices.text: Intel, because the name has neither `a` nor `p`
choices.why: Right. There is no letter for Intel, so its absence is the answer.

choices.text: Arm, because `s` stands for Cobalt
choices.why: `s` means any Premium SSD; Arm is `p`.

choices.text: The name does not say, so you have to look it up
choices.why: It does say, by leaving the letter out: a name without `a` or `p` is Intel.

prompt: How much memory does `Standard_D4ds_v5` have, and where does the name say so?
hint: Memory is not one of the pieces of the grammar a D size carries.

choices.text: 150 GiB, the `d`
choices.why: 150 GiB is the local temporary disk the `d` adds, not memory.

choices.text: 4 GiB, the number
choices.why: The number is vCPUs, not gibibytes.

choices.text: 16 GiB, which the name does not state: it follows from 4 vCPUs at the D family's 4 GiB each
choices.why: Right. Memory comes from the family's ratio.

choices.text: 32 GiB, because `ds` doubles the memory
choices.why: `d` and `s` say nothing about memory; `m` is the letter for more of it.

prompt: In `Standard_M8-2ms`, the 8 is the size it is built on and the 2 is the number of vCPUs left switched on. Microsoft calls a size like that ___.
hint: The opposite of unrestricted.

prompt: A colleague copies `--size Standard_DS2_v2` from the example in `az vm create --help` into a new deployment script. What is the problem?
hint: Read the version, and remember the lifecycle stages.

choices.text: The CLI will refuse it, because examples in help are placeholders
choices.why: The CLI checks nothing about the size; it would send it as written.

choices.text: Dsv2 is End of Life, retiring in 2028
choices.why: Right. It is set to retire in 2028, nothing warns you, and a new machine belongs on a current version.

choices.text: No problem, since Microsoft keeps its own help current
choices.why: Help text is written once and copied for years, and this example shows it.

choices.text: The capital S makes it a storage-optimised size
choices.why: Storage optimised is the `L` family. The capital `S` is the old way of writing the series name.

prompt: The nightly sales report needs about 12 GiB of memory and one busy vCPU. Why is `Standard_E2s_v6` a better fit than `Standard_D4s_v6`?
hint: Both have 16 GiB. Count the vCPUs.

choices.text: The same 16 GiB on two vCPUs, not four
choices.why: Right. The job runs out of memory first, so you buy memory and stop paying for three idle vCPUs.

choices.text: E is a newer, faster family than the D family
choices.why: A family is a ratio, not a rank; both are v6.

choices.text: D sizes stop at 8 GiB of memory
choices.why: A `D4s_v6` has 16 GiB; D sizes reach hundreds.

choices.text: E sizes come with a local disk for the report
choices.why: A local disk is the `d` letter, and `E2s_v6` does not carry it.

prompt: `vm.bicep` declares `vmSize: 'Standard_D3ps_v6'`, a size that does not exist, and `bicep build` prints nothing. Why?
hint: Look at the type the compiler printed when it was given a number.

choices.text: The compiler checked the size against the live list for `brazilsouth` and found it there
choices.why: The compiler contacts nothing; it has no list of sizes at all.

choices.text: Bicep checks sizes just when the file declares an image too
choices.why: No property makes another one checked; the image is simply another property.

choices.text: Warnings about sizes are switched off by default
choices.why: There is no such warning to switch off. The `2` produced one at once.

choices.text: In this API version `vmSize` is typed `null | string`, so any text passes
choices.why: Right. A typo in a size name is one of the mistakes the compiler cannot catch.

prompt: Order these sizes from the least memory per vCPU to the most.
hint: Divide memory by vCPUs: the letters l and m move a series along the line.
trap: M8ms has the most vCPUs of the four and still comes last, at about 27 GiB for each one.

prompt: Match each workload to the family it belongs on.
hint: Which resource runs out first?

pairs.left: A relational database holding its working set in memory
A Cassandra node reading its own local NVMe at high rates
A staging server idle most of the day
A weather model on many cores

prompt: You move the order API from `Standard_D2s_v5` to `Standard_D2ps_v6`. What has to be true first, and what do you gain?
hint: What does the `p` change about the programs that run, and about what a vCPU is?

choices.text: No change is needed; you gain a local disk
choices.why: A local disk is `d`, and it is not in this name. The `p` changes the instruction set.

choices.text: The subscription needs Arm enabled; you gain twice the memory
choices.why: Both sizes have 8 GiB, since both are D. What changes is the processor.

choices.text: An arm64 image; each vCPU becomes a whole core
choices.why: Right. The shop's Python runs on Arm, and two vCPUs become two Cobalt 100 cores instead of two Intel threads.

choices.text: The disks need converting to Premium SSD; you gain network bandwidth
choices.why: Both names carry `s`, so both already take Premium SSD, and the `p` is not about the network.

prompt: A database on `Standard_D2s_v5` is slow, its processor mostly idle, and its four Premium SSDs are each rated well above 3,750 IOPS. What is the likeliest limit?
hint: There are two limits on a disk's I/O, and the program gets the lower.

choices.text: The disks are too small and should be replaced by larger ones
choices.why: Larger disks have higher ratings of their own, and the machine's cap still applies on top of them.

choices.text: The network, because small sizes share 12,500 Mbps
choices.why: The four smallest sizes do share that ceiling, and a disk-bound database with an idle processor points to the disk cap instead.

choices.text: The processor, which needs a compute-optimised family
choices.why: It is mostly idle; buying processor would not help.

choices.text: The machine's own 3,750 IOPS cap
choices.why: Right. The cap counts all its disks together; a size up raises it, and a faster disk does not.

prompt: A `Standard_B2s_v2` (2 vCPUs, base 40%) runs both vCPUs at 70%. How many credits does it spend per hour?
hint: Credits per minute = (base × vCPUs − CPU used × vCPUs) / 100; then times 60.

prompt: A `Standard_B4s_v2` (4 vCPUs, base 40%, holds at most 2,304 credits) starts a load test with a full bank and runs all four vCPUs at 100%. After how many hours is it held to its base?
hint: Work out the credits spent per minute, then per hour, then divide the bank by it.

prompt: One CPU credit pays for one vCPU at 100% for one ___.
hint: It is why an idle B2s_v2 banks 48 an hour.

prompt: A database licensed per vCPU needs the 256 GiB and the disk limits of `Standard_E32s_v5` and uses about eight vCPUs. What does `Standard_E32-8s_v5` change?
hint: Constrained sizes keep everything but the active vCPUs.

choices.text: The machine costs a quarter as much, with the same licence
choices.why: Microsoft prices a constrained size as the original; the saving is the licence.

choices.text: It keeps the 32 vCPUs and limits the database to eight of them by configuration
choices.why: Twenty-four vCPUs are switched off and not available to the machine at all.

choices.text: Eight active vCPUs, same memory and disks, a quarter of the licence
choices.why: Right. Same price for the machine, a quarter of the licence.

choices.text: It has 64 GiB, a quarter of the memory, to match the vCPUs
choices.why: The memory stays at 256 GiB; that is the point of the size.

prompt: A staging server on `Standard_B2s_v2` (2 vCPUs, base 40%) idles at 10% for ten hours overnight. How many credits does it bank?
hint: (base × vCPUs − CPU used × vCPUs) / 100 per minute, for 600 minutes.

prompt: A `Standard_B2s_v2` (base 40%, banks 48 an hour when idle, holds at most 1,152) runs both vCPUs at 100% for 12 hours every day and idles for the other 12. It starts with a full bank. What happens?
hint: Work out what one busy half-day spends and one idle half-day banks.

choices.text: The bank holds steady, since the nights bank more than the days spend
choices.why: Twelve idle hours bank 576 and twelve busy hours spend 864, so each day ends 288 lower.

choices.text: The bank falls by 288 a day, and from the third day it runs dry during the busy hours and is held to 40%
choices.why: Right. The third busy period starts with 576 credits and spends 72 an hour, so it lasts 8 of the 12 hours.

choices.text: Azure moves it to a D size automatically when the bank is empty
choices.why: Nothing resizes it; Microsoft documents holding it to its base as the outcome.

choices.text: It is billed for the processor above 40% at a surplus rate once the bank is empty
choices.why: The documentation describes no surplus billing for the B family; the outcome is throttling.

prompt: Match each additive letter to what it says.
hint: Lower case, after the number.

pairs.right: Less memory per vCPU than the family's usual
The least memory per vCPU in the series

prompt: Two `Standard_D2s_v5` or one `Standard_D4s_v5`, at an illustrative rate that scales with vCPUs. What decides it?
hint: If the money is equal, what is left?

choices.text: How you want it to fail: two survive the loss of either, one gives one copy more room
choices.why: Right. With the money equal, the choice is about failure and growth in smaller steps.

choices.text: The price, since two machines cost more than one
choices.why: At a rate that scales with vCPUs, two D2s cost exactly what one D4 costs.

choices.text: The network, since the D4 gets twice the bandwidth
choices.why: Both are listed at 12,500 Mbps; the small sizes share that ceiling.

choices.text: The memory ratio, which is better on the larger size
choices.why: The ratio is 4 GiB per vCPU at every size of the series.
